1:
Chrysostom asks why there is a second letter at all, and answers from the first: Paul had written that he hoped to come shortly, the visit had not happened, and so instead of coming he consoles by writing — to a man grieving at his absence and oppressed by the cares of a government just taken up. He generalises it: even great men set at the helm feel the strangeness of the position and are overwhelmed as by waves of business. Barnes and Clarke both stop here to settle when it was written. Each lists the authorities against himself — Lardner, Lightfoot and Hammond for the first Roman imprisonment, Paley and Macknight for a second — and each comes down for the second, on Paley's ground and Macknight's. In the earlier letters Paul confidently expects release and asks Philemon to prepare him a lodging, whereas here he is ready to be offered; and Onesiphorus had to seek him out very diligently before finding him, which fits close confinement rather than the hired house and single soldier of the first. Clarke adds a rejoinder more of character than of argument: to say Paul merely despaired at first and grew hopeful later reflects little honour on him, making him a man subject to alarms.

On the apostleship by the will of God, Ellicott hears the note the whole letter is written in: the office came apart from any merit of Paul's own, he neither aspired to it nor wished for it, and the appeal to the sovereign will is in harmony with the calm resignation breathing through the epistle. Calvin asks instead why the lofty titles are used at all in writing to one man already convinced, and answers that Timothy was not the only person in view: being near death, Paul claims the authority belonging to his public character. Henry keeps it plainer: the commission was merely of God's good pleasure, by a grace Paul professes himself unworthy of. On the next phrase Ellicott presses the preposition, which should be rendered for rather than according to, so that it states the object of the appointment, to publish abroad the promise of eternal life — and he notes what it means that a letter written under expectation of death opens on life. Robertson agrees, adding that the life in Christ Jesus takes in the present as much as the future. Calvin uses the phrase to reach backwards: the promise was given to the fathers in ancient times, so the faith of men under the law must have looked toward Christ, what the promises held being suspended until it was exhibited in him.

The epithet has changed since the first letter, and two voices notice. Ellicott observes that Timothy was there Paul's own or genuine son and is here his beloved son, and reads the change as feeling rather than doctrine: despite the urgent request that Timothy come with all speed, Paul knew these lines were in reality his farewell. Robertson turns the substitution into evidence of another kind, recalling that Paul had already called Timothy beloved when writing to Corinth, and treating that as incidental but strong proof that Paul is the writer here — an argument holding for each of the Pastorals, since the affectionate relation they assume is attested in Acts and the earlier epistles. Gill narrows the sonship twice: not natural but spiritual, and not on the ground of having converted him but of having instructed him. Calvin closes with something no commentator is obliged to say. Whenever we read this letter, he urges, let Paul's condition come before our eyes, a man looking for nothing but to die for the gospel as its standard-bearer; and he adds, for his own part, that this epistle has been more profitable to him than any other book of Scripture.
3:
What the thanks is for is not obvious, because a long parenthesis stands between the verb and its object. Ellicott says the point has been much argued and rewrites the sentence to settle it: Paul thanks God when he calls to remembrance the unfeigned faith of Timothy, everything between being an aside. Robertson notices the idiom is not the one Paul normally uses for giving thanks but a rarer phrase meaning I have gratitude. Then comes a flat disagreement about the ancestors. Barnes takes them to be the patriarchs and holy men of former times, Paul's forefathers as a member of the same nation, and draws the conclusion he wants from it — that Paul's religion was not a different one from theirs but the same carried out and perfected, the Old Testament and the New being essentially one. Ellicott denies precisely this: not Abraham and Isaac and the patriarchs, but the members of Paul's own family, whose devotion he had inherited as a family tradition. Clarke and Wesley take the pure conscience together in one direction, that Paul had always aimed to please God according to his light, even in the time when through ignorance he persecuted the church.

Whose tears, and shed when, nobody can quite fix. Clarke lists three possibilities and declines to choose between the parting from the Ephesian elders, the hour when Timothy was first taught Christ crucified, and some interview otherwise unrecorded. Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott settle on the last parting, Ellicott citing the scene at Miletus not as the occasion but as evidence that Paul left strong men weeping; Wesley suggests the tears were shed often and not only then. Ellicott has no patience with Hofmann's alternative, that they were merely Timothy's grief on hearing by letter of the arrest, which he calls singular and far-fetched. Gill supplies the practical reason for the longing, that Timothy's work at Ephesus was finished and Paul at Rome was now without any assistant, and Barnes thinks the desire to see him is probably why the letter exists at all. Barnes also stops to defend the weeping itself, on the ground that religion is not intended to make us stoics or savages, and takes the passage as proof that a very pure and warm friendship may hold between an old man and a young one, and that its warmth is not diminished by the near prospect of death.

Barnes and Clarke arrive independently at the same argument from the two named women, and it is an argument about the documents rather than the doctrine. Luke reports that Timothy's mother was a Jewess who believed and his father a Greek, but never names her or the grandmother; Paul names both and never mentions the father. Neither account was built from the other, and the coincidence is undesigned, which both take after Paley as evidence for the genuineness of each. Clarke presses two further inferences: that the historian was not particularly acquainted with the family and the apostle evidently was, and that passing the father over in silence suggests he was either still unconverted or by now dead. On the names Clarke observes that both are Grecian and indeed heathen, so Timothy's mother, Jewess though Luke calls her, was Hellenist by birth; Ellicott adds that Lois is the familiar Lais and Eunice the equivalent of Victoria, and raises the guess that the family were kinsfolk of Paul, Lystra lying no great distance from Tarsus, before dismissing it as an ingenious thought with no data behind it. Two voices converge on how Paul knew: Robertson notes the word means a reminder received from someone else rather than a recollection of one's own, and Ellicott thinks some particular instance of Timothy's faith had reached the prison. Wesley takes the verb for dwelling and presses it: not a word for a transient guest, only for a settled inhabitant.
6:
Ellicott supplies a motive the others leave implicit: Timothy was cast down by the imprisonment, knowing his master's career was ending, and sinking at the prospect of fighting alone at Ephesus without the man who had guided Gentile Christianity for a quarter of a century. The verb is agreed on by everybody — not rouse in general but kindle, fan into flame, the word built on the live coal and then on the bellows — and Henry makes it fire under the embers. What follows from the image is not agreed. Clarke draws the sharpest inference: a fire not frequently stirred and fed goes out, so if Timothy had not continued a daily worker with God he would have received the grace of God in vain. Barnes puts the same thing more temperately, that however rich the gifts God bestows they do not grow of their own accord but need cultivating by our own care. Ellicott brings Chrysostom in to say it is in our power both to quench the Spirit and to fan it, then passes on Wordsworth's suggestion that Paul had in mind the Roman law commanding that the eternal flame of the public hearth be watched, whose failure was an omen of disaster and whose watchers were severely punished.

Then the old difficulty returns, because the first letter said the presbytery's hands and this one says my hands. Three answers are given. Ellicott takes it as one act in which the presbytery at Lystra were joined with the apostle. Barnes agrees it was one act and argues the point at length: the words prove Paul took part but not that he acted alone, and they are exactly what any member of an ordaining body would naturally say — an aged minister reminding a young one that his own hands had been laid on him, which is a tender and solemn appeal rather than a claim of sole authority. Henry separates them into two occasions. The presbytery ordained him; Paul's hands did something else and earlier, conferring the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost, since Henry reckons that none but apostles had the power of giving the Spirit. Robertson declines the question and reads the possessive as feeling, Paul having a deep personal interest in Timothy. Barnes closes by denying what the passage is often used to establish, that any mysterious influence passed from the hands of the ordainers imparting a holiness Timothy had not before; what was given, he says, the next verse names.

The word rendered fear means cowardice, and four voices say so. Clarke adds a variant nobody else reports, that some manuscripts read bondage rather than cowardice, and then sets the verse against Sinai: the law was given with a terrible majesty that bred fear until even Moses trembled, while the gospel came in mildly, nothing in it forbidding. The last of the three gifts divides the room. Ellicott and Robertson render it self-control, Ellicott describing the power that keeps passions, desires and impulses in wise subjection. Barnes makes it soberness of judgement, a mind well balanced and not feverish, seeing things in their just proportions. Henry makes it quietness of mind, and adds the shrewd reason that we are often discouraged by creatures of our own fancy which a solid thinking mind would answer at once. Clarke reports the narrow rendering of self-possession only to reject it as too small, holding out for a clear understanding, a sound judgement, a rectified will and holy tempers — the whole soul harmonised. Wesley alone arranges the three into a figure: power and sobriety are two good extremes and love is the tie between them, preventing the two bad extremes of fearfulness and rashness. Barnes grounds the middle term in experience: love of country and wife and children makes the most timid bold when they are assailed.
8:
Wesley makes the join from the verse before: when fear is banished, evil shame flees away too. Chrysostom locates the shame in method rather than nerve: nothing is worse than measuring divine things by human reasonings, and a man who tries it falls from the rock as surely as one who would look at the sun with human eyes is injured for trying. That, he says, is how Marcion and Valentinus came to be ashamed of the divine economy, which was never a subject for shame but for glorying. Then he turns it over. Death and chains are in themselves matters of reproach, but once the cause is added and the mystery seen rightly they are full of dignity — that death saved a perishing world and joined earth to heaven, and those chains converted many. He will not let the charge stop at endurance: the text says not merely be unashamed of the sufferings but be partaker of them, so it is not enough not to blush at them, one must not blush to experience them. Clarke reaches the same point by a colder road, observing that we acknowledge friends readily while they are in credit and grow quiet when they fall, and citing Cicero that a true friend is discerned in adverse circumstances.

On the phrase closing the verse Ellicott answers against the obvious reading: the power of God here is not the strength we receive for suffering but the power already displayed towards us in our calling and salvation, so the argument runs from what has been done for us to what may be asked of us. Clarke reads the same words as a promise of proportion: a man never has more affliction than he has grace to bear, and a load carried by God's strength cannot be oppressive. What follows is the ground of both. Barnes takes the calling as holy in its own nature and leading to holiness, and presses the negative: our works have nothing to do with inducing God to call us, nor could the eternal purpose have been formed on works foreseen. Gill finds a salvation earlier still, a providence attending the elect from birth and a chain of ordinary circumstances — the fixing of their habitations, the bringing of them under such a ministry — leading to the effectual calling. Ellicott brings two witnesses, Chrysostom on a purpose originating in God's own goodness with none advising him, and Calvin's compressed version — if God chose us before the creation of the world he could not have considered our works, which had no existence when we ourselves were not.

Then the great verse, where the room agrees on the force but divides on the novelty. Clarke insists the doctrine of eternal life was not unknown to the Jews, who found it in their prophets and borrowed nothing from Christians, so the gospel cannot be said to have first disclosed it; what it did was demonstrate what had existed only in promise. Barnes takes the opposite line and proves it from the heathen, gathering Cicero calling the hope of a future state a conjecture of ages, and Socrates at his own death hoping to go hence to good men but declining to be positive, since which of us is in the better state, the living or the dead, God only knows. Of the resurrection of the body, he adds, they had no conception at all. Ellicott and Robertson supply the words themselves: abolished means rendered inoperative rather than destroyed, and the second noun is incorruption rather than immortality; Wesley puts the same thing devotionally, that the sting is taken away and the thing turned into a blessing. Ellicott closes on a point of Greek that is almost an epigram — death carries the article, being a known and ruling power, while life and incorruption stand without it, having only just been revealed.
11:
Ellicott catches what is strange about the three titles arriving here. A solitary prisoner awaiting death, deserted by his friends, rehearses with solemn emphasis the dignities his Master had given him in the church — because he means his last charge to go out with the full authority of an apostle, while admitting in the next breath that these very sufferings came upon him through the position that authority put him in. Clarke supplies the sense of the words: the first is herald, the second means sent immediately from God to man, and the third is the one whose business is to instruct, the Gentiles particularly. Gill makes the appointment twofold, from eternity in the counsel of God and in time by the church at Antioch, and then permits himself a judgement — if ever there was a preacher of the gospel Paul was one, who preached purely, powerfully, publicly, constantly and boldly.

The famous clause is commonly read as though Paul were saying he knows in whom he has believed, and Robertson will not have it: the relative is a dative governed by the verb, the antecedent is simply unexpressed, and this is not an indirect question at all. Paul knows the person he has trusted. Having settled the grammar the two who address it disagree about who that person is, Robertson taking it of Jesus Christ and Ellicott referring it to God the Father; Ellicott also presses the tense, whom I have trusted and still trust. Clarke keeps to the ground of the confidence rather than its object, saying he is acquainted with the goodness and mercy and power of Christ and knows he cannot confide in him in vain.

What the deposit is has divided commentators of every age, and Clarke sets out the three answers without choosing between them: his life, put into Christ's hands to be received again at the resurrection; his soul, given to a faithful Creator whom wicked men cannot reach; or the gospel itself, which God will preserve and cause to be proclaimed by others when Paul has sealed it with his blood. Wesley says flatly that it is the soul. Ellicott says the same and is the only voice to bring evidence: the imagery is probably from the psalm Paul knew, into thy hand I commend my spirit, whose Greek uses this very verb; Josephus, writing in the same age, calls the soul a deposit in a passage against suicide; and Philo, near enough a contemporary, uses the identical expression — both passages, he notes, quoted at length by Alford, who nonetheless concludes slightly differently. Robertson turns the word into a picture, a deposit as in a bank, the bank of heaven that no burglar can break, and notes that the verb means to guard against robbery or loss. Barnes uses the same confidence to explain why trouble need not disturb a man: one shipwrecked who sees his child safe beside him on the shore will care little that a casket of jewels went overboard, and a man's great interests may be safer in a prison than a palace. On the closing phrase Barnes observes that it needed no further description — the early Christians spoke and thought of it so constantly that that day alone identified it, the day for which all other days were made.
13:
The noun means an outline, the plan of a building or a picture, and Barnes canvasses what has been made of it — Grotius calling it an exemplar fixed in the mind, Calvin requiring adherence to the doctrine in its form as well as its substance, an archbishop taking it for the profession of faith made at baptism. Barnes then argues that whatever Paul gave Timothy was not written, and gives an unusual reason: had such a summary existed on paper it would have been reckoned inspired and would have found its way into the canon, since almost nothing would have been more carefully preserved; besides, the text says Timothy heard it. Chrysostom draws the opposite conclusion from the same fact. Paul taught by word as well as by letter, many things were delivered without writing, and we must not therefore suppose anything in doctrine was imperfectly spoken; he pictures Paul as an artist who has impressed an image on his pupil, fixing in his soul a rule and outline of all that pleases God, so that Timothy need not go elsewhere for examples when everything has been deposited within him. Barnes ends where Chrysostom would not, allowing a brief summary of doctrine as a convenience but denying it binding authority over anyone's conscience.

Gill takes the verse as a rule for theological vocabulary and states it with care. Words are not to be strived over for their own sake; but when a word has long served to convey a just idea of truth it should not be lightly given up, though nowhere syllabically in Scripture, unless a better can replace it — and it must be held most stubbornly when the evident aim in dropping it is to set aside the truth it carries. He names the words he has in mind: trinity, unity, essence, person, imputed righteousness, satisfaction. Clarke argues the same necessity from the other direction: no man was left to invent a religion after his own mind, since God alone knows what God can be pleased with. Ellicott suspects a particular fear behind the charge, that the glosses of the false teachers would get a readier hearing once the hand of Timothy's old master was cold and his heart had ceased to beat.

Ellicott then notices something easy to miss, that the deposit has changed hands between the two verses: in the earlier one Paul committed something to God, in this one God has committed something to Timothy, and Robertson says the same in a sentence — God has also made an investment in Timothy. What the trust contains is variously named: the gospel by Clarke and by Gill, doctrine to be transmitted by Barnes, wholesome doctrine by Wesley, the treasure of the Catholic faith by Ellicott. On how it is kept there is no dispute at all. Chrysostom explains why the command names the Spirit: a soul entrusted with things so great is not sufficient to keep them, since there are many robbers and thick darkness and an adversary who chooses his own hour. He answers with the psalm — except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain — calling the Spirit our wall and castle and refuge. He then raises the difficulty himself: if the Spirit dwells in us and is our guard, why any commandment at all? Because we may hold it fast and not banish it by evil deeds. Ellicott turns the point outward: the deposit is not preserved by weak compliance with the scruples of false teachers, nor by timid accommodation, nor by yielding a little here and a little there. Cyril of Jerusalem quotes the verse for a different purpose, as one of his proofs that Paul and the apostles were full of the Holy Ghost.
15:
How wide the desertion was is disputed. Clarke restricts it to the Asiatic Christians then at Rome, who found the apostle in disgrace and thought it dangerous to own him, and denies that any general defection of the Asian churches can be meant; Wesley reads it the same way. Ellicott rejects that reading though Chrysostom held it, and takes the plain sense: the forsaking happened in Asia itself, large numbers of Christians and perhaps whole churches repudiating their connection with the father of Gentile Christianity, so that what had often been threatened at Corinth occurred while he lay waiting for death. He then narrows the geography rather than the event: Asia strictly taken would include Mysia and Phrygia and Lydia and Caria, and a defection that wide is improbable and unattested, so Paul probably used the old Homeric sense, the country about the Cayster. Barnes draws a quieter inference from the same words: Timothy must have been in that region when the letter reached him, since otherwise he could not be supposed to know it, and all must be general, because a faithful exception is named two verses later. Robertson declines the question outright, saying it is not known what incident is meant.

On the two men named, Barnes and Robertson reach the same verdict from opposite temperaments. Robertson notes that nothing else is known of them except this shameful item; Barnes turns it into a warning, that it is a sad thing when the only record of a man, the only evidence that he lived at all, is that he turned away from a friend. Barnes also reports the tradition that they were of the seventy and ended as followers of Simon Magus, calls it little more than conjecture, and adds the shrewder observation that the pretended lists of the seventy seem to have been made by taking every name incidentally mentioned in the sacred books and not otherwise accounted for. Wesley alone lets the desertion land as an injury. What, he exclaims, from Paul the aged, the faithful soldier, now the prisoner of Christ — and calls it a glorious trial wisely reserved for the time when he stood on the borders of immortality; then he reaches for the picture of Francis Xavier inscribed apostle of the Indies, forsaken of all men, dying in a cottage.

Against them stands one man, and whether he was alive when Paul wrote turns out to be a doctrinal question. Ellicott and Robertson judge him recently dead, Ellicott because mercy is asked for his house rather than for him and because of the phrase about that day, Robertson adding that if he lost his life for visiting Paul it had probably just happened. Barnes and Henry take the opposite view. Paul would not have offered prayer for him if he were dead, says Barnes, and the argument for praying for the dead rests on an assumption for which there is no evidence; Henry puts the same objection as a question — who told them Onesiphorus was dead, and can it be safe to ground a doctrine and a practice of that importance on a mere supposition? Ellicott, who has conceded the premise Barnes denies, handles the controversy with more care than either: Theodoret and Chrysostom held Onesiphorus to be living, and wrote centuries before any dispute on the point arose; and the words ask no more than that an act of unrequited love be remembered when the books are opened — so that pressing the one text in the New Testament that touches the question, and whose sense is not agreed, is extremely precarious. On the kindness itself the word means to cool again, and Ellicott will not let it shrink to food and blankets: it covers the visits, the contriving after Paul's release, and a noble disregard of what a man risked by open intimacy with a prisoner charged with treason.
17:
The searching is what all five voices dwell on, because it implies something about the prison. Clarke infers a close and private confinement so that the apostle could be found only with great difficulty, and Ellicott says outright that this must have been a far more rigorous captivity than the one at the end of Acts, where Paul lived in his own hired house with a single guard; Robertson adds that Onesiphorus apparently did it at the risk of his own life. Barnes turns the point on the reader instead: not everyone, even among professors of religion, would take the trouble in a great and splendid city to search out a Christian brother, or even a minister, who was in prison — and he expects this man to be among those told at the last that they came to Christ in prison. Clarke ends on two proverbs rather than an argument, that pure love feels no loads, and that here was a friend who sticks closer than a brother.

The next verse says the Lord twice, and what to do with the repetition divides the room. Ellicott declines the easy solution that the phrase had become a formulary and the second occurrence went unnoticed, and keeps both strictly: the first is Christ, which is what the title always means in Paul, and the second is the Father, to whom judgment at the last day is elsewhere ascribed. Clarke reports that same construction as one opinion — a prayer to the Father for grace that the man may find mercy at the hand of Christ the Judge — but thinks the doubling probably a Hebraism, citing three places in Genesis and Exodus where the idiom occurs, and reads the whole simply as a wish that he be saved now by grace and receive mercy then unto eternal life. Gill runs through the possible constructions and settles for none. Robertson hears an echo none of the others catch: Onesiphorus sought and found Paul, and the prayer is that he may find mercy from the Lord as he found the apostle.

Two smaller observations come from the last clause. Ellicott notes that the Greek for ministered has prompted the suggestion that Onesiphorus held the office of deacon at Ephesus, and refuses to build on it, calling the inference from one general expression precarious; Robertson points out that Paul writes not that Timothy knows but that he knows better, the only comparative of its kind in the New Testament, since these were things done at Ephesus where Timothy was and Paul was not. Then both Barnes and Clarke close the chapter by standing back from it. Barnes sets down what the chapter shows: a holy man in prison and near death, forsaken by the friends he might have relied on, his mind nevertheless calm and his one anxiety that a younger man should never shrink from the gospel; and against the general apostasy, one friend who never swerved, which proves that when friendship and religion meet in the same heart each strengthens the other. Clarke's summary is warmer and stranger. He runs through the life — the perils, the superabundant labours, the track of light left wherever he went — and then the old age, neglected, in prison and in chains, unshaken, feeling no evil and fearing none, because sin had lost its power and death its sting. He finishes with a poet's lines on the man who could know the causes of things and trample fear and inexorable fate and the roar of greedy Acheron beneath his feet, and observing that this was the happiness of which heathenism could speak but which it could not reach, not knowing the source it must come from.
